https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/cultur.text: Merging the everyday and the elevated, Leo Ray manages to capture the simplicity of everyday motifs - painting dogs, cats, birds, and people in slightly distorted images with classical art references.A known colorist, painter, graphic artist, and small-scale sculptor, he was born in Vilnius, Lithuania, in 1950 (then part of the USSR), where he studied theoretical physics at Vilnius University and art at Vilnius Academy of Arts. After making aliyah in 1991, he lived in Tel Aviv. Shortly thereafter, the same year, he showed his paintings in a group exhibition in Tel Aviv and entered the local art scene. Since then, he has had many individual shows in Israel and abroad. For over 30 years, up to the pandemic, he taught art at Art School, Ein Vered, and BASIS School of Sculpture, Beit Yanai, where he also headed the painting program from 2006 to 2014. He paints constantly, every day, exploring infinite painting, in which one canvas is a continuation of the previous one. During the interview for the Magazine, he showed me 99 paintings, like a chain of stories. Renaissance, classical, often referenced in Ray's modern, eclectic compositionsThe Renaissance and classical art are often referenced in Ray’s modern, eclectic compositions. When he paints in colors, which is what he is known for, his colors are vibrant and defined. When he steps away from them, he paints just in black and white. His brushstrokes are very characteristic, and he seems to play with layering oil, acrylic, and gouache. Many define his art as naive and childlike; during the interview, he told me he disagrees with those opinions. But he agreed that his art can bring out the child inside of us. In my view, Ray’s paintings put a smile on viewers’ faces. That’s why I wanted to meet this artist and introduce him to The Jerusalem Post’s wide audience of readers. In the dark times we live in, Ray brings a basic way of joy into his work.We met in his modest art studio, filled with brushes and paintings, located between car repair shops and workshops, in the industrial zone of Tel Aviv. Leo Ray welcomed me with tea; he was covered with paint, taking a break from the endless painting to talk to me.When I first saw your painting three years ago, I literally smiled! A big yellow dog was smiling from the canvas back at me. Recently, at the Freshpaint Art Fair, I saw a collection of your paintings and smiled again. They make me happy. Is it your goal to make people happy?Absolutely. Life can be very difficult, and I think one of the great functions of art is to make people happy in this or other ways. I think that, for example, the art of Charlie Chaplin is no less important, great, and artistic than some, let’s say, tragedies. I think that laughter and joy are very valuable things.Thank you for doing it. And my other thought when I saw your paintings was that they’re like illustrations for children’s books. Was it right or not? No, I never illustrated children’s books, and some people say that my style is childish. I absolutely disagree.I wouldn’t say it’s childish, but I think when you paint dogs, birds, cats, and people in not-so-realistic proportions, in a dreamlike way, it awakens the child within us.Yes, of course! I think the child in us doesn’t die before we die. That’s a great sentence! Have you painted this way all your life? Well, that’s a question: if I’ve changed. Yes, I did. One of my friends said that the painting itself changed in a way; that the process of painting became more fun over the years.In your case, or in general? How come?In general. For example, if you compare a painting by [Johannes] Vermeer to a painting by Jackson Pollock, I think Pollock had more fun. Interesting, I didn’t think about it this way… and in your case?My fun is mainly discovering what appears in the painting, what is building up in a painting I am working on.So, you don’t plan the painting; it comes in the process? Sometimes I do plan the paintings and make sketches, but usually, when I start the real one, it changes everything. We’re sitting in your studio, and there are lots of brushes, from small to extremely large ones. Do you choose them, play with them, like with instruments?Of course, brushes are very important instruments, and every brush does what it does. It has individuality. My professor once said that there is no bad brush. And he is right, because [even] a used brush makes what it makes. No new brush can make the same. So, I’m using different kinds of brushes for different kinds of, let’s say, strokes.And you also use different kinds of paints. I paint in oil, acrylic, and gouache (when on paper). And I use Indian ink. I’m trying to be democratic with the painting. I don’t think the use of a kind of material describes the style of a painting. What would you say describes your style? I would say that I do things in a concise way. I like short sentences. I like short lines in poetry. And I like short jokes. So, this kind of brief message is my style. Brief messages. And why those very defined colors, like yellow and red? Because I love them.Trained in calligraphy, 'that's why I use brushes'In opposition to your colorful world, which you are known for, you also paint only in black and white. Which kind of paint do you use for this? Sometimes I’ll use acrylic, but if I work on paper, it’s Indian ink. What do you like about black and white?In the academy, I had a leading professor who was teaching calligraphy, so I’m a little bit trained in calligraphy, and so I love it a lot. That’s why I use brushes.In your paintings, there are repetitive characters.Yes. My principal male character is a nobody. So he can have any name you want to give him. I cannot say anything about the women. This is interesting. You said the man is nobody, and women have some character? They always have some character, and they are always very tempting. And they are beautiful and gracious. Do the dogs, birds, and cats in your paintings have names? No. I don’t give names to cats and dogs. They have to think about that themselves. Are there, or were there, real cats and dogs in your life? Yes. I came here with a cat.From Lithuania, from the collapsing Soviet Union? A few months before the collapse. I came from the Soviet Union formally. I had to refuse Soviet citizenship and so on… So, I came with my cat.What was his name?It was Otto, because of the perfect symmetry of the name and the perfect symmetry of the cat. Your cat, in the painting that I’m looking at, has a symmetric face - but its legs are not symmetric... It depends on the viewing angle. If it’s a little bit twisted, you don’t see the symmetry.Your paintings often have rich textures. When do you decide to apply layers of paint? For example, this painting is mostly flat, but the child’s face is covered in more layers of paint, and the cat’s eyes are more layered.It is not a rational decision. It’s a feeling that I need here to do something. Every color, every texture has its meaning. What meaning does it have to you? The meaning is mysterious. Painting is a mysterious thing. I once said that the ultimate purpose of a painter is to deepen the mystery. And I was very surprised to find out not very long ago that almost the same words were said by Francis Bacon. So, I think like everything that is in the world, like astronomy, physics, mathematics, chess, love, and painting. These are mysterious things that can be explained, only to have a purpose to spoil them. The paintings we are talking about, despite the fact that you don’t want to describe them as naive, have naive and surrealistic elements. But you also paint in a more realistic style.Yes, there was a period when I tried to combine the realistic images with my traditional style, [by this I mean] the flat, two-dimensional, bright-colored things, and see if they go together well. I have a series of the so-called Rembrandt women, where I combined paintings made from some images from Rembrandt, more or less in a realistic style, with my images.You also portrayed Rembrandt himself in your paintings.Yes, sometimes. Apart from paintings, you also sculpt. Is it very different from painting for you?It’s a different kind of thinking; it’s a different kind of three-dimensional thing you have to plan. You grew up in Lithuania when it was still part of the Soviet Union and began your artistic education as a teenager. Could you tell me a little about that?When I was 14, I asked my parents if they would allow me to attend an art school, and they did. Can you tell me something about your parents, your family? My parents were Jewish, of course. Many generations of Vilnius Jews. Both of my parents were scientists in the field of chemistry. My sisters also went into science. So there were no art traditions from home. And what do you recall from the way you were taught art in that school? At this art school for children worked [at the time] very good Vilnius artists. I met some outstanding personalities. It’s a pity that as a child, you didn’t fully understand with whom you were dealing. The way of teaching was rather traditional. Every day we had to draw cubes, and we had to draw plastic casts of ancient, let’s say, gods and philosophers. Well, it was very hard for me as a child.Why was it hard? Well, drawing with a pencil, because when you don’t understand what you are doing, the teachers put some models, some still lifes, and you had to draw them.But despite that, you continued your art education afterward.Yes, I did. It was a master’s five-year program at the Academy of Art in Vilnius. But I’m learning all my life, whenever I start a new painting. You came to Israel in 1991, with the big wave, the aliyah of Soviet Jews. From a very different reality. Was it a cultural shock for you to come here? Yes, but now it’s gone. What was your first impression of the local art scene when you came here? I don’t remember. I don’t think that I saw the art scene when I came here. I was busy with very different things. But I started painting, of course, immediately. As if I knew what was going to happen.I came here in April 1991, and in September (same year), there was a big exhibition of newly arrived painters, organized by the Association of Artists in Tel Aviv. Two galleries chose my works from the photographs.We’re talking about the pre-Google era, so was the fact that they heard about you already a success?No, they didn’t hear about me. It was advertised everywhere; you just had to send photos and your materials to the Association of Artists. And there, the commission, the jury, chose what they liked.And since then, you... Since then, I somehow entered the art scene. One gallery in Tel Aviv chose me, and I worked with that gallery for four years.When did you start teaching in Israel? I started teaching maybe in 1993. It was the private art school established by my friend and sculptor David Zundelovitch. I taught at this school, later called the BASIS School of Sculpture, Beit Yanai, until COVID. When you taught art, what was your message to the students? I didn’t have one message. I taught them mainly composition. I think that composition is the most important thing that the art student has to learn to understand the principles, and then you can do it with anything that you want. Skills come while working, in the process. Speaking of process, please tell me about your infinite painting practice? When you say infinite painting, does it mean that each painting has a story that continues on the next canvas?Absolutely, yes. When I came up with the idea that I am moving on with the painting, I’m adding canvases one to another, and it’s an infinite thing. I thought about other infinite things, and I understood that infinite things contain everything. So, I tried there to paint things that I can paint. There are abstract pieces, there are realistic pieces, and there are realistic people.For example, these wrapped paintings [Ray pointed] are my infinite painting, so-called infinite painting, which now has 99 canvases joined together. It was exhibited in Israel and in the US. Ninety-nine? That’s very impressive! Do you paint every day? Yes. I come to the studio in the morning or early afternoon. It’s the best time to paint. Best light.Are you preparing a new exhibition right now? No, I’m just working on separate works. At the end of our conversation, I have to ask how you speak Polish, my native language, so well (we spoke on the phone before the interview, and you surprised me). Polish is a completely different language from Lithuanian and even from Russian. Where did you learn it?At first, as a child, we had a Polish-speaking nanny there, a woman who helped my mother. But I really learned it when I was young and wanted to read books that weren’t published in the USSR. There was a bookstore in Vilnius that sold books in Polish and German, and I chose Polish to read them. I really like the language. [He smiled.]Dziekuje [thank you, in Polish] for talking to me.Dziekuje for visiting me at my studio!www.leorayart.com

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: This handout image released by the Grand Canyon National Park Service via X shows remnants of stone bridge pylons along Bright Angel Creek after a flash flood on 29 August 2026. Photograph: J Thompson,handout/National Park Service/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen This handout image released by the Grand Canyon National Park Service via X shows remnants of stone bridge pylons along Bright Angel Creek after a flash flood on 29 August 2026. Photograph: J Thompson,handout/National Park Service/AFP/Getty Images Arizona Grand Canyon braces for more storms after flash flood leaves one person dead National park officials say body of a man, 46, was recovered and about 15 others remain missing or unaccounted for Associated Press Mon 31 Aug 2026 08.26 EDT First published on Mon 31 Aug 2026 08.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Grand Canyon area braced for more rain and thunderstorms on Monday after a flash flood that left one person dead and about 15 others missing or unaccounted for – with scores of visitors evacuated and the only water pipeline for tourists and residents destroyed. Emergency water restrictions that began on Monday prevented tourists from staying overnight at lodges and hotels within the park. Year-round residents were asked to conserve water. A flood watch was in effect. Visiting the Grand Canyon – a crown jewel of the US national park system – can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding that accompanies the monsoon, or rainy, season. Clear days can give way quickly to thunderstorms and downpours. “With deep monsoonal moisture in place and already saturated soils in some locations, an elevated risk of flash flooding will be in place through Monday,” the National Weather Service (NWS) said early in the day. The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River , the National Park Service (NPS) said without providing additional details. The flooding Saturday in Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the river, led to more than 60 people being airlifted from the canyon’s depths. The park service asked anyone with details about hikers or campers still unaccounted for to get in touch. The Arizona department of public safety helped with additional evacuations on Sunday. “These measures are crucial for ensuring the safety and sustainability of water resources,” the park said in a statement. Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with fellow physicians and a park ranger when heavy rain started falling on Saturday. “We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” he said. Later, as they made their way toward Phantom Ranch, a colleague shouted “Up, Up, Up, Up!” as a 4ft (1-meter) debris wall headed toward them and they ran up into a patch of cacti, he said. They were rescued by helicopter late on Saturday after making it to the Phantom Ranch area, he said. Torrents of water wiped out footbridges over the creek and altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and extending an existing river rapid or creating a new one. The flood was a blow to an enduring effort to modernize the pipeline that serves 6 million visitors a year and roughly 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village. “Heaven help us if the whole thing down there at the bottom has to be reconstructed,” said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University. “Where are they going to get the money?” Halting overnight stays at the park because of a lack of water is rare, although the pipeline frequently has failed over the years. While the Grand Canyon has large storage tanks for potable water on the South Rim, they won’t be refilled while the pipeline is out of service. A $208m rehabilitation of the pipeline and upgrades to the associated water delivery system started in 2023, with the park service calling it a crucial investment to ensure the park can meet the needs of residents and visitors. The project was expected to be completed next year. In unrelated flooding, officials in San Antonio, Texas, on Sunday reported a pair of deaths related to a severe storm there two days earlier. Police said a 46-year-old woman died after being caught in rushing water in San Pedro Creek north of downtown, Texas Public Radio reported . A person with that woman made it out the situation safely, police said. Separately, police said a man in his 50s was found at Woodlawn Park on Sunday morning. The woman’s death is being investigated as a drowning while the man’s death is considered a possible drowning, police said. https://www.travelerstoday.com/articles/.text: More than 18.5 million Americans described themselves as digital nomads in 2025, according to MBO Partners' 2025 nomad research, a figure that has more than doubled since 2019. Most of them do not work from a beach. The ones who tried to live in a legal grey area in Europe cannot anymore: since April 10, 2026, the European Union's Entry/Exit System has automatically recorded every non-EU traveler's entries and exits across all 29 Schengen countries, eliminating the smudged-passport workaround that an entire generation of remote workers quietly depended on. What remains after that shift is a lifestyle that is more viable than ever for people who engage with it properly, and more expensive and legally exposed than the influencer version suggests for those who don't.Nobody Actually Works on the BeachThe image that sells the lifestyle, a laptop balanced above the waterline with an unobstructed ocean view, fails on contact with reality. Sand damages keyboards and vents. Direct sunlight makes screens unreadable. Beach WiFi, where it exists at all, cannot reliably sustain a video call. Travel professionals who track nomad infrastructure describe the actual setup as a beach-town lifestyle in which work happens at a co-working space or fiber-connected apartment, and the ocean is a place you go afterward.The connectivity requirement for a professional workday is not negotiable. A single active user needs a minimum of 25 to 30 Mbps with stable upload speeds for video conferencing and cloud access, according to internet speed guidance for remote workers. The actual challenge is not raw speed but reliability: packet loss, latency spikes, and shared café bandwidth during peak hours consistently derail calls far more than advertised download numbers suggest. A 100 Mbps fiber connection at a co-working space outperforms a faster but shared café connection in practice, which is why serious remote workers pay for dedicated co-working memberships in nomad hubs rather than hopping between coffee shops.In Bali, Canggu's residential internet providers advertise significantly faster speeds than they deliver in practice, and intermittent neighborhood-wide power outages happen regularly, according to nomad infrastructure comparisons. Chiang Mai's fiber providers, by contrast, reliably deliver much faster connections to most central apartments. The difference matters if your job involves daily video calls or large file transfers.Can You Work in Europe on a Tourist Visa After the EU's Biometric Border System?Technically, remote work for a foreign employer has always been a legal grey area on a Schengen tourist visa, and overstaying the 90-day limit was always prohibited. What changed on April 10, 2026, is enforcement. The European Commission confirmed that the EU's Entry/Exit System went fully operational at every external border crossing point in all 29 Schengen countries. The system replaces passport stamping with biometric registration, collecting fingerprints and facial images and automatically calculating each non-EU traveler's remaining permitted days. Overstays that previously went undetected because of inconsistent manual checks are now flagged automatically.Commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration Magnus Brunner described the system as designed to "identify overstayers, prevent irregular movements, and combat document and identity fraud." Since its introduction, the EES has logged more than 52 million crossings and flagged over 27,000 entry refusals.The consequences of overstaying are now certain and documented. Even a short overstay can result in fines and a multi-year ban from the entire Schengen Area, according to EU immigration guidance. The record enters the Schengen Information System and remains visible to border officers across member states. A single overstay can also affect future visa applications to countries outside Europe.The critical distinction that most coverage misses: travelers who hold a national digital nomad residence permit from a Schengen country are tracked as residents, not short-stay visitors, and the 90-day enforcement does not apply to them. Spain, Portugal, Greece, Croatia, Germany, Estonia, and the Czech Republic all offer such programs as of 2026, according to immigration tracking sources. If you are working remotely in Europe on a tourist entry, the grey area is now binary: you are either compliant or you are tracked.For practical guidance on navigating EES border procedures and queue times at European airports this summer, see TravelersToday's coverage below.What Countries Have Legal Visas for Remote Workers in 2026?More than 50 dedicated digital nomad visa programs existed globally in 2026, with additional remote-work permits that function similarly, according to immigration tracking sources. The programs vary significantly in income requirements, stay length, and tax treatment.Income thresholds run from zero in Georgia, where many nationalities can stay visa-free for up to a year, to several thousand dollars per month in Estonia and Japan, according to multiple immigration guides. Simpler entry points include Portugal's D8 visa, Spain's digital nomad residence permit, Croatia's program (which exempts foreign income from local tax for the duration), and Thailand's Destination Thailand Visa, which allows stays of up to 180 days per entry with renewal. Italy's digital nomad visa, launched in March 2024, requires annual income of at least €28,000 and a permesso di soggiorno application within eight days of arrival. Bulgaria became the latest European entrant in 2026, requiring a minimum annual income threshold and targeting workers earning outside Bulgaria.Most programs share a key tax benefit: foreign-sourced income earned while on the visa is exempt from local income tax, though the rules and applicable thresholds vary by country and require verification against official sources before any financial planning. Holders of these visas are tracked by the EES as residents and are not subject to the 90-day short-stay enforcement. The visa is the difference between operating legally and operating in a zone that EU border technology can now detect automatically.For nomads considering Thailand as a Southeast Asia base, an important policy shift has already taken effect: Thailand reduced its visa-free stay period from 60 to 30 days.How Much Does the Digital Nomad Lifestyle Actually Cost?The geoarbitrage calculation, earning in dollars or euros while spending in baht or rupiah, still produces meaningful savings in 2026. The math is just less dramatic than the five-year-old blog posts suggest.In Chiang Mai, Thailand, the typical all-in cost for a solo digital nomad runs approximately $1,200 per month according to nomad cost trackers, covering a private condo, co-working access, meals, and transport. A comfortable lifestyle with a better apartment and regular dining out runs $1,800 to $2,500. Da Nang, Vietnam, which has emerged as the 2026 value leader in Southeast Asia, comes in at $700 to $1,100 per month including co-working access, per nomad cost researchers compiling Numbeo city data. Bali's bootstrapping tier starts around $1,170 to $1,390 per month in a shared villa or co-living arrangement, with Canggu rents having climbed significantly year-on-year according to property market reporting.Chiang Mai carries one constraint rarely featured in nomad promotion: a smoke season running roughly February through April when PM2.5 air quality regularly spikes into the unhealthy and hazardous range, well above the WHO safe level according to air quality monitoring data. Nomads who base in the city typically treat it as a nine-month destination and relocate during the smoke period.Accommodation in Bali's most popular nomad areas now carries its own compliance risk. The Indonesian Ministry of Tourism set a licensing deadline for all accommodation providers operating on Online Travel Agency platforms. Thousands of properties that had not obtained required business licenses faced delisting from Airbnb, Agoda, Booking.com, and Traveloka from August 1, 2026, according to compliance reporting citing Indonesia's Ministry of Tourism and property advisors citing Indonesian accommodation data. Nomads booking accommodation in Bali should confirm properties hold current licensing status before committing to longer stays.The Tax Trap Most Nomads Miss Before They Leave HomeGeoarbitrage's financial logic depends on keeping tax exposure manageable, and the rules are more layered than most first-time nomads expect.Most countries trigger local income tax residency after 183 days of physical presence in a calendar year, according to international tax guidance. Countries that have set that threshold, including Spain, Portugal, Estonia, and Greece, apply rates that can reach 30% or more on income above local thresholds. Some destinations are specifically designed to avoid this: Croatia's digital nomad visa exempts foreign income from local tax, Uruguay applies territorial taxation where foreign income earned abroad is typically exempt, and Malta does not tax foreign income that is not remitted into the country.American nomads face a structurally different problem. The United States is one of only two countries globally that taxes citizens on worldwide income regardless of physical residence, according to international tax advisors. The Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE) allows qualifying US citizens abroad to exclude up to $132,900 of foreign earned income from federal income tax for the 2026 tax year, provided they meet the Physical Presence Test (330 full days outside the US in a qualifying 12-month period) or the Bona Fide Residence Test, per FEIE guidance for expat filers. But the exclusion covers earned income only. Dividends, capital gains, and interest remain fully exposed. And self-employment tax at 15.3% applies on self-employment income regardless of where you live, even when the FEIE reduces income tax to zero. For freelancers, this is frequently the calculation that makes the economics look different on paper versus at tax filing.A complication that catches departing Californians in particular: the California Franchise Tax Board residency rules allow the state to pursue income tax on worldwide income for years after a person has left if significant ties remain, such as property ownership, a spouse in the state, or an active professional license, according to tax advisors who have handled such cases. Simply counting fewer than 183 California days does not establish non-residency under the state's domicile and ties framework.Loneliness, Burnout, and the Social Cost of Constant RelocationThe financial and legal planning is the part most guides cover. The social cost is the part that pushes people home.Surveys of digital nomads consistently find that approximately 40% report feeling lonely often or always, and 77% report having experienced burnout from their work at least once, according to data compiled by Passport Photo Online. A peer-reviewed study published in Media, Culture & Society in 2025 by researchers including Cristina Miguel and Christoph Lutz documented nomad loneliness through interviews: digital nomads accumulate more social contacts than most people encounter in years, but the contacts never deepen past a certain point because one person in every pair is always about to leave. The result is a social paradox where a person can feel profoundly isolated while being surrounded by acquaintances.Loneliness and travel fatigue are the top two reasons digital nomads stop traveling and return home, according to statistics from A Brother Abroad. Neither shows up consistently as the biggest daily struggle, which tends to be client retention and finding new work. They accumulate over time instead, eroding the lifestyle's appeal in a way that is not visible on travel photography.Co-working spaces and purpose-built nomad communities have emerged as the primary social infrastructure, offering a built-in layer of like-minded contacts that a randomly booked apartment does not provide. Some communities now coordinate travel routes digitally, matching nomads heading to the same city in advance rather than leaving connection to chance encounters. The infrastructure helps, but it does not solve what researchers describe as the core tension: a lifestyle built on movement and a social life that requires staying somewhere long enough for relationships to deepen.What the Working-from-Anywhere Lifestyle Actually RequiresThe lifestyle has genuine infrastructure now that it lacked a decade ago: more than 50 dedicated visa programs, a co-working industry that has professionalized around nomad needs, and AI tools that approximately 89% of nomads report using to manage the friction of distributed work, including language barriers, time zone coordination, and code generation for solo developers, according to nomad lifestyle reporting citing MBO. The tooling has arguably done more to make the lifestyle sustainable for solo freelancers than any visa program has.What the tooling does not replace is planning. The people who make it work tend to share a common infrastructure checklist: a legal visa for stays longer than a few weeks, a co-working membership or confirmed fiber-connected accommodation rather than a reliance on café WiFi, verified connectivity speeds before committing to a lease (requesting a Speedtest screenshot from a landlord is now standard practice in nomad communities), international health insurance that holds up for a 12-month stay rather than a short-trip policy, a clear picture of their home country's tax obligations, and at minimum an understanding of which countries trigger local tax residency at the 183-day threshold.The 36% of US nomads who are currently working remotely without formal employer consent, according to MBO Partners data cited in nomad lifestyle reporting, represent a segment with compound exposure: return-to-office mandates that have tightened across major employers since 2024, and a Schengen border system that now tracks location automatically. Neither risk is unmanageable, but neither can be resolved by not thinking about it.The beach is still there. The people actually working are in the co-working space up the road, running a Speedtest before every important call.

Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGE View image in fullscreen Callum Robinson, 33, and his brother Jake, 30, from Perth, Australia, were camping in a remote beachside area when they were robbed and killed. Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGE Mexico Alleged killers of Australian surfers and American friend go on trial in Mexico Three men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024 Agence France Press in Ensenada Mon 7 Sep 2026 13.29 EDT Last modified on Mon 7 Sep 2026 13.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The alleged killers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot in 2024 have gone on trial in the border resort where the three were murdered. The Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were shot dead after being robbed in Mexico’s violence-hit Baja California . They were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked. Their bodies were found hidden on a cliff. Tourist killings expose fragmentation of organised crime at the heart of Mexico’s extraordinary violence Read more The Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the trial. “It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” Martin Robinson told reporters as he entered the court with his wife, Debra. “We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” he said. View image in fullscreen Jake (left) and Callum (right) with their parents, Debra and Martin Robinson. Photograph: Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation Three men are on trial for homicide. The girlfriend of one of the accused was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery . The crime sparked outrage and sadness in Australia and the United States. Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad was killed a few months before he was due to marry. Other foreign tourists have previously been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast. Two Australian surfers were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa . Their bodies were later burned. https://www.mediafax.ro/english/nazare-r.text: Nazare: Romania in talks with DFC to establish a Romania-US investment fund „Romania has proposed—and is currently in discussions with the DFC—the establishment of a Romania-US investment fund that would bring together the Investment and Development Bank, American private capital, and other funding sources, focusing on energy, digital infrastructure, critical minerals, and other strategic Romanian assets,” Nazare stated in a Facebook post. The announcement follows discussions held in New York with representatives including Ben Black, Executive Director of the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC). The goal of these meetings is to mobilize the largest possible volume of private investment from both Romanian and American capital sources. The Romanian state has been in talks with American financiers—including both DFC and Exim Bank representatives—since last year. „Discussions continued on the sidelines of the Atlantic Council conference in Athens in November 2025, where I met with representatives from both the DFC and US EXIM. ​​This spring, at the Three Seas Initiative Summit in Dubrovnik, meetings with the DFC took place at both the level of President Nicuşor Dan and at a technical level between representatives of the Investment and Development Bank and the DFC,” Nazare said. The DFC is one of the primary instruments the US uses to mobilize private capital for global investments. With over $40 billion invested globally, the institution finances projects in energy, infrastructure, critical minerals, technology, telecommunications, and other strategic sectors. „The Strategic Partnership between Romania and the United States already rests on a solid foundation regarding political and security aspects. Over the past year, we have worked to strengthen its economic dimension as well. The goal is clear: more American capital in Romania, more technology, and increased investment and production capacity developed here,” Nazare concluded. The discussions took place on the sidelines of the Romanian delegation’s visit to New York for the 81st UN General Assembly. The delegation was led by President Nicuşor Dan.
